headline: US tech stocks surged last night with GOOG up 3.6% ahead of earnings, but PLS dropped 3.7% today as lithium sentiment stays weak — meanwhile the US-Iran conflict escalates and the RBA decision looms large.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG had a strong session last night, up 3.6% to $370.21 USD. Markets are building anticipation ahead of Alphabet's earnings release next week — analysts expect strong growth, and the stock has been outperforming the broader market. The overall tech rally on the NASDAQ also helped lift it.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO climbed 2.85% last night, riding the broader NASDAQ tech rally. GTA 6 excitement remains a key driver — the title is expected to be a monster revenue event for Take-Two. GTA V's online cash cards are also noted as a continuing quiet revenue earner.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft rose 2.78% last night as tech broadly rallied on the NASDAQ. All eyes are now on July 29 earnings — analysts are divided on whether Microsoft can deliver the AI-driven growth the market is pricing in. It's a make-or-break result for the stock near-term.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS fell 3.66% today to $4.47 — the worst mover in your portfolio this session. There was no single fresh catalyst; it's been ongoing weakness in lithium sentiment and cautious market positioning. The stock is down over 33% from your buy-in, but the broader lithium recovery thesis is still debated — it's nearly tripled over the past year from its lows.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI.AX dropped 2.68% today to $16.00. This is likely profit-taking or sector rotation on the ASX — the AI ETF space can be volatile even when the underlying US AI stocks are doing well, as local pricing lags. You're down 15.3% overall on this position.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG barely moved today, down just 1 cent to $76.00. Essentially flat — this diversified ETF is doing exactly what it's designed to do: smooth out daily noise. Nothing to worry about here.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged down 0.09% today — essentially unchanged. Emerging markets are watching the US-Iran conflict and broader global risk closely, but no major moves today. The IMF did upgrade China's GDP outlook through 2027, which is a mild positive for this ETF longer term.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS was flat today at $532.83, reflecting yesterday's modest S&P 500 gains already priced in. The US total market ETF is your steadiest position and is sitting on a small 3.3% gain overall.

watch_today.title: GOOG earnings next week — big moment approaching
watch_today.detail: Alphabet reports earnings next week and expectations are high — analysts are forecasting strong growth and the stock has already run up 3.6% last night in anticipation. For a long-term holder this is exciting, but also a reminder that a miss could cause a short-term pullback. Sit tight and let the business results speak.

watch_today.title: Microsoft July 29 earnings — the real test for your MSFT position
watch_today.detail: MSFT reports on July 29 and the stakes are high. Multiple analysts are calling it a 'crisis of confidence' moment — the market wants to see AI investment paying off in actual revenue. MSFT is up 2.78% last night but is still down 10.7% from your buy-in price. As a long-term holder, this earnings result could be a turning point either way — hold through it and see what the business delivers.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX down 3.7% today — still a bumpy ride for lithium
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped another 3.66% today to $4.47, taking your total loss on this position to around 33.7%. There's no fresh company-specific news — it's ongoing soft lithium market sentiment. The long-term lithium story (EVs, battery storage) remains intact, but the timing is uncertain. Unless your conviction in lithium has fundamentally changed, hold and be patient — but keep your eyes on Chinese EV demand data as the key indicator.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX down 2.7% today — short-term noise, long-term thesis intact
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF slipped 2.68% today despite US AI stocks rising last night — this is an ASX pricing lag/rotation effect rather than a structural problem. You're down 15.3% overall on this position, but the AI sector story is strong and accelerating (NVIDIA launching new Jetson Thor computers, AI regulation ramping up globally). Hold for the long term.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision coming — watch for mortgage and market impact
watch_today.detail: The RBA's next rate call is being closely watched by brokers and lenders. Industry is divided — some expect a cut, others a hold. A cut would boost ASX growth stocks and ease pressure on household budgets. No decision today, but keep an eye on any announcement this week as it will move the ASX and the Aussie dollar.

watch_today.title: US-Iran conflict escalating — oil and global markets at risk
watch_today.detail: The US has reimposed a blockade and stepped up strikes on Iran, which has threatened to halt Middle East energy exports. If Iran follows through, oil prices could spike sharply — currently WTI crude is holding around $79.53 USD but that could change fast. Higher oil = higher inflation globally = pressure on interest rates. Worth watching closely this week.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict is escalating seriously, the IMF has revised its global economic outlook, the White House is considering releasing classified intelligence on Chinese election interference, and Germany is pushing back on perceived US political meddling.

stories.title: US reimposed blockade on Iran and steps up strikes — Tehran threatens to cut off Middle East energy exports
stories.why_it_matters: The US has reimposed a naval blockade on Iran and escalated military strikes, and Tehran has responded by threatening to shut down Middle East energy exports entirely. Iran says it 'never welcomed war' but is not backing down. If energy exports from the region are disrupted, oil prices could spike globally — that means higher petrol prices here in Australia and renewed inflation pressure, which would complicate the RBA's plans to cut rates. UNICEF has separately warned that the conflict has already pushed over 23 million additional children into poverty risk globally.

stories.title: IMF July 2026 World Economic Outlook: 'Global Economy at War and at a Tech Crossroads'
stories.why_it_matters: The IMF's July 2026 World Economic Outlook paints a sobering picture: the global economy is being squeezed by ongoing conflicts (especially in the Middle East) and is at a pivotal moment with AI technology reshaping industries. The IMF did upgrade China's GDP outlook through 2027, which is a mild positive for Australian exporters and emerging market investments. But the broader message is caution — geopolitical risk is the dominant force for global growth right now.

stories.title: White House weighs releasing classified intelligence on China's alleged election interference
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is reportedly considering declassifying intelligence that allegedly shows China interfered in the 2020 US election. This would be an explosive geopolitical move — directly accusing China publicly of election meddling would escalate US-China tensions significantly. For Australian investors, deteriorating US-China relations could hit trade, hit emerging market ETFs like VGE, and rattle global markets. Trump is also planning a prime-time speech on 2020 election allegations, keeping political tensions very high in Washington.

stories.title: Germany warns the US against interfering in its upcoming elections
stories.why_it_matters: Germany has officially warned the United States not to interfere in German elections after the US announced a grants scheme that Berlin says could be used to influence political outcomes. This is a significant diplomatic flashpoint between two major NATO allies. It reflects growing tension between Europe and the Trump administration and signals that US-European unity — already strained — is being tested further.

stories.title: FIFA breaks a rule for the first time ever for the 2026 World Cup Finals
stories.why_it_matters: FIFA has broken one of its own long-standing rules for the 2026 World Cup Finals — the first time in history this has occurred. While the specific rule wasn't detailed in the article text, it's significant enough that it's generating major global sports news coverage. The 2026 World Cup is already one of the biggest sporting events ever planned, with 48 teams across the US, Canada and Mexico.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 was essentially flat today, barely moving from yesterday's close. Last night on Wall Street, both the S&P 500 and NASDAQ had solid sessions — tech was the star with GOOG, MSFT and TTWO all up over 2.7%. The Aussie dollar crept slightly higher to just under 70 US cents. Gold dipped slightly and oil is barely changed.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil barely moved despite US-Iran tensions escalating — watch this space carefully.

indicators.name: Gold

politics.summary: The Albanese government is moving on two fronts: a new AI blueprint sparking debate about data centre rules and AI copyright, and fresh modern slavery laws that could expose Australian companies to criminal charges over global supply chains.

stories.title: Albanese's AI blueprint sparks calls for a data centre building freeze
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government has released an AI blueprint that also includes new rules for data centres — including a requirement for them to generate more clean energy than they consume. The response has been divided: the tech industry broadly supports Labor's push to regulate AI, saying the 'self-regulation era is closing', but some groups are calling for a moratorium (a pause) on new data centre construction until the full regulatory framework is in place. The government is also tackling AI copyright — who owns content that AI is trained on. This is shaping up to be a major policy area heading into 2027.

stories.title: Australian companies could face criminal charges for forced labour in their supply chains
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government's new Modern Slavery laws would make Australian companies criminally liable if forced labour is found in their overseas supply chains. This goes significantly further than existing reporting obligations — it shifts from 'disclose and explain' to 'fix it or face prosecution.' Companies that source goods from high-risk regions (like parts of South-East Asia or China) will need to do serious due diligence. This could particularly affect retail, manufacturing and resources sectors.

stories.title: RBA rate decision looms — industry split on next move
stories.why_it_matters: The next RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) rate decision is drawing near and the mortgage industry is split on what comes next. Brokers and lenders are placing bets — some expecting a cut, others a hold. A cut would mean lower repayments for millions of Aussie mortgage holders and would generally be positive for growth-oriented ASX stocks. A hold would keep pressure on household budgets. Worth watching closely — the decision will directly affect your cost of living and the broader ASX.

ai.summary: Australia's AI policy debate is heating up with new data centre laws and calls for tighter regulation, while NVIDIA has launched major new hardware for robotics and edge AI, and top Google researchers are reportedly being lured away to rivals.

stories.title: NVIDIA launches Jetson Thor computers to power mainstream robotics and edge AI
stories.why_it_matters: NVIDIA has announced the Jetson Thor — a new line of compact, powerful computers designed to bring AI and robotics capabilities to everyday devices and edge locations (think factories, warehouses, vehicles — anywhere that isn't a big data centre). This matters because it signals AI is moving out of the cloud and into the physical world at scale. NVIDIA remains at the centre of the AI hardware revolution, and products like this drive ongoing demand for their chips.

stories.title: The 'London Rule' — why top Google AI researchers are jumping ship to Anthropic
stories.why_it_matters: A so-called 'London Rule' — referring to an internal Google policy that limits researcher autonomy — is reportedly a major reason why top AI researchers are leaving Google for rivals like Anthropic (the company behind the Claude AI). This talent drain matters because the AI race is fundamentally a people race — the best researchers tend to build the best products. For GOOG holders, it's worth keeping an eye on whether Google can retain the talent needed to stay competitive.

stories.title: Australia's new data centre laws: centres must generate more clean power than they consume
stories.why_it_matters: Under new Australian laws, data centres will be required to generate more renewable electricity than they actually use — effectively forcing them to become net clean energy producers. This is a world-first type of regulation that puts significant obligations on big tech companies operating in Australia. It will increase the cost of running data centres here, but also accelerates Australia's push into renewable energy infrastructure. AI companies looking to expand in Australia will need to factor this in.

stories.title: Industry backs Albanese's AI push but warns 'more is needed'
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's AI industry is broadly supportive of Labor's new AI regulation framework, with leaders saying 'the era of AI self-regulation is closing' — meaning companies can no longer be trusted to police themselves. However, they're also urging the government to go further and faster, warning that without strong rules, Australia risks being left behind as other countries (the EU, the UK, the US) move quickly on AI governance. This signals a significant shift in how AI will operate commercially in Australia over the next few years.

sport.summary: NRL Round 20 kicks off tonight with Panthers v Broncos at CommBank Stadium. The finals race is heating up with multiple clubs jostling for top-eight spots. In the AFL, Essendon has been fined over umpire contact and the score review system is getting an upgrade by Round 24.

stories.title: NRL Round 20 finals race: 'Keep winning' as clubs jostle for top eight
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL finals race is getting serious heading into Round 20, with several clubs separated by just a few competition points. Tonight's Panthers v Broncos clash at CommBank Stadium (7:50pm AEST) is a big one — Penrith are always a finals threat and the Broncos need wins to stay in the eight. Your Gold Coast Titans host the Sea Eagles on Sunday at Cbus Super Stadium at 2pm.

stories.title: AFL: Essendon fined for umpire contact — and score review is getting 'new toys' by Round 24
stories.why_it_matters: Essendon has been hit with a fine from the AFL for umpire contact — details of the incident weren't available but the club will feel the financial hit. Separately, the AFL's football boss has revealed that a major upgrade to the score review system — featuring 'new toys' including enhanced camera technology — will be in place by Round 24. The aim is to eliminate the controversial goal/no-goal calls that have frustrated fans and clubs all season.

stories.title: Wallabies tapping into a resurgent fanbase
stories.why_it_matters: The Betoota Advocate — with its trademark tongue-in-cheek style — is reporting that the Wallabies are experiencing a genuine fanbase resurgence, with crowds apparently rediscovering their passion for Australian rugby. It's a welcome story for Rugby Australia, which has been working hard to rebuild interest after some lean years. Whether it translates into results on the field remains to be seen.
